hints: Look carefully at the scale bar and notice where $1 \text{ nm}$, $100 \text{ nm}$, $1 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$ and $100 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$ sit, then ask yourself if a bacterium is closer in size to a virus or to a plant cell.
Recall the typical diameter of a bacterium like E. coli, about $1 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$ long, and see which bracket is centred on $1 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$.
walkthrough:
**Read the size scale**

Think of this as a zoom from very tiny to visible. Range A is $1 \text{ nm}$ to $100 \text{ nm}$, range B is centred on $1 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$, range C is centred on $10 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$ to $100 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$, and range D goes up to $1 \text{ mm}$.

Remember:
$$1 \text{ }\mu\text{m} = 1000 \text{ nm}$$

**Recall typical cell sizes**

Viruses are tiny, about $20$ to $100 \text{ nm}$. Prokaryotic bacterial cells are much larger, typically about $0.5$ to $5.0 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$, with many around $1 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$. Eukaryotic animal and plant cells are larger still, about $10$ to $100 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$.

**Match prokaryotes to the bracket**

Range A is too small, that is virus size. Range C and D are too large, that is eukaryotic cell and tissue size. Range B, spanning from about $100 \text{ nm}$ up to a few micrometres and centred on $1 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$, is just right to include most prokaryotic cells.

options.A: Too small for cells. $1 \text{ nm}$ to $100 \text{ nm}$ is the size range for viruses and large molecules, not bacteria.
options.B: Correct. This range is centred on $1 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$ and covers about $0.1$ to a few micrometres, which includes most prokaryotic cells.
options.C: Too large for prokaryotes. $1 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$ to $100 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$ is the typical range for eukaryotic cells such as animal and plant cells.
options.D: Far too large. $100 \text{ }\mu\text{m}$ to $1 \text{ mm}$ includes very large eukaryotic cells and structures visible with the naked eye.
